summary: Describes service classes configured with Differentiated Services and recommends how to use and build them using DSCPs, traffic conditioners, per-hop behaviors and active queue management. It states that no particular DSCP use is strictly required. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: On a busy road, buses and ambulances get special lanes. This suggests how to set lanes for different kinds of internet traffic.

questions: what is the telephony service class
how many diffserv service classes are there
subtitle: A set of 'project plans' for building twelve DiffServ service classes with consistent code points, queues and policers.

tldr.problem: Differentiated Services is a toolkit that is powerful but hard for a non-expert to use, and networks that mark and treat traffic differently from each other lose end-to-end quality of service.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines twelve service classes (two for network control, ten for user traffic) and recommends a DSCP, an edge conditioner, a PHB, a queuing style and an AQM setting for each.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational memo, not a standard, and it says no particular DSCP, PHB or AQM is strictly required. It has been updated by RFC 5865 and RFC 8622.

today: RFC 4594 is an Informational memo and is listed as updated by RFC 5865 and RFC 8622; it has not been obsoleted. The RFC itself says it does not specify an Internet standard of any kind.

sections.title: Why Service Classes Are Needed
sections.content:
The RFC compares the Differentiated Services specifications to a workshop toolkit of band saws and drill presses. In an expert's hands there is no limit to what can be built, but a non-expert who only wants a bookcase needs project plans. This document is meant to be those plans for network administrators.

A service class is a set of traffic that needs specific delay, loss and jitter behavior from the network. Classes are based on what applications need, so new applications can be mapped into an existing class. The RFC defines twelve classes, two for network operation and ten for user traffic, but expects administrators to implement only a subset.

The text states plainly that there is no intrinsic requirement that particular DSCPs, traffic conditioners, PHBs or AQM mechanisms be used for a given class. It argues that applying them consistently is useful for policy and interoperability. Only the Default Forwarding Standard class is REQUIRED; all other classes are OPTIONAL.
sections.plainLanguage: The tools for sorting internet traffic are like a big box of woodworking tools. This paper hands you ready-made plans, so you can build a bookcase without being a master carpenter.

sections.title: The Building Blocks: Queues, AQM, Conditioners and PHBs
sections.content:
The RFC recaps the DiffServ pieces it builds on. A priority queue empties the highest-priority queue first, which limits delay and variation in delay but must avoid starving lower queues. A rate queue (such as Weighted Fair Queuing or Weighted Round Robin) empties each queue at a specified rate.

Active Queue Management (AQM) drops or marks packets to manage queue depth; the canonical example is Random Early Detection (RED), which uses a minimum and a maximum threshold. Traffic conditioners measure arriving traffic at the first router and drop, mark or shape it, normally with token bucket meters. The RFC names a single token bucket for CS and EF, and usually two meters for AF, following RFC 2698 or RFC 2697.

The DSCP is a number in the range 0..63 placed in an IP packet. Half of the values are earmarked for standardized services and half are for local definition. A PHB (per-hop behavior) combines these mechanisms into the treatment a class receives. Four basic behaviors are used: Default Forwarding (DF), Assured Forwarding (AF), Expedited Forwarding (EF) and Class Selector (CS).
sections.plainLanguage: Some lines are for VIPs and some are for everyone else. A gatekeeper checks each person's ticket, and someone watches that no line gets too long.

sections.title: The Twelve Service Classes and Their Markings
sections.content:
Traffic is split into network control and user traffic. Network control has Network Control (routing) and OAM (configuration and management). User traffic has ten classes: Telephony, Signaling, Multimedia Conferencing, Real-Time Interactive, Multimedia Streaming, Broadcast Video, Low-Latency Data, High-Throughput Data, Standard and Low-Priority Data.

The RFC groups the user classes into four application categories: application control, media-oriented, data and best effort. It tags each with its flow behavior (elastic, rate adaptive or inelastic) and an end-user rating from ITU-T G.1010 (interactive, responsive, timely or non-critical).

The recommended markings are listed in the figure below. The RFC says it is RECOMMENDED that the mapping between classes and code points be preserved end to end. Class names and order imply no priority; they are only reference names, and administrators MAY choose different names.

Default Forwarding and Class Selector 0 (CS0) give equivalent behavior and share the code point 000000. A packet marked with a DSCP the network does not support SHOULD be forwarded using the Standard class.
sections.plainLanguage: The traffic is sorted into twelve boxes, like voice calls in one, movies in another and email in a slow one. Each box gets a colored sticker so every town sorts the same way.

sections.title: How Each Class Is Configured
sections.content:
Sections 3 and 4 give a recipe per class. Network Control (CS6) carries routing traffic such as OSPF, BGP, ISIS and RIP, uses rate queuing, and is not open to user traffic. Telephony (EF) SHOULD use the EF PHB of RFC 3246 with a priority queue, because voice packets are inelastic and must be forwarded as soon as possible.

Voice and other inelastic flows are protected by admission control and by policing at ingress, so the priority queue cannot be overrun. Signaling (CS5), Real-Time Interactive (CS4) and Broadcast Video (CS3) use CS PHBs with rate queuing and policing by a single-rate meter with burst control.

The AF-based classes (Multimedia Conferencing, Multimedia Streaming, Low-Latency Data and High-Throughput Data) use the RFC 2597 PHB with a three-color marker and AQM per DSCP. Standard uses DF with AQM, and Low-Priority Data uses CS1 with the PHB of RFC 3662.
sections.plainLanguage: Each box has its own rules. Emergency calls skip the line, big downloads wait their turn, and the gatekeeper makes sure nobody sneaks into the fast line.

sections.title: Three Deployment Examples
sections.content:
The RFC expects administrators to start with three or four user classes and add more as needed. Example 1 is a provider offering reliable VoIP, a low-delay assured-bandwidth data service and normal Internet service. It uses six classes: Network Control, Standard, Telephony, Signaling, Low-Latency Data and OAM.

Example 2 grows that network by four classes (Real-Time Interactive, Broadcast Video, Multimedia Streaming and High-Throughput Data) to add desktop video conferencing, IPTV and on-demand movies, and network storage and backup. Example 3 is an enterprise network that needs nine classes. In every example, packets with an unsupported DSCP SHOULD be forwarded as Standard.
sections.plainLanguage: A small town might need only a few lanes. As it grows and adds a train and a stadium, it adds more lanes without redoing the whole road.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document describes policy, and the RFC says that if it is implemented as described, the network does nothing it had not already allowed, so no new security issues should arise. A policy can still be applied wrongly, and the network SHOULD detect and correct that.

A well-known flaw is that bandwidth reserved for one service, such as voice, can be used by another service or by attack traffic. This is inherent in DiffServ, which depends on appropriate packet markings. Where reservation or priority queuing is used, authentication and flow admission are recommended. Some classes, such as Network Control, are not permitted to users at all, and such traffic should be dropped or remarked by ingress filters.
sections.plainLanguage: If anyone can walk into the VIP lane just by wearing a VIP sticker, the lane stops working. So the doors need guards who check who is allowed in.
